sections.html:
Arkansas works on a two-year rhythm. Values and millage rates are fixed in the assessment year, and the money is collected the year after. The state Department of Finance and Administration oversees all 75 counties, but assessing, collecting and distributing are local jobs.

During the assessment year, county assessors, clerks, equalization boards and judges settle values. School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set millage, and the quorum court formally levies it. During the collection year, county clerks, collectors and treasurers send bills, take payments and pass the money along. Each assessment year doubles as the collection year for the year before, so an owner is always living in two cycles at once.

Business personal property is assessed by May 31. Homeowners care mostly about the notice in summer, the hearing windows in late summer and fall, and the October 15 due date.

sections.h2: What millage rate will a house pay?
sections.html:
Across counties the state average is 48.80 mills, built from school, city and county rates set after the 2025 school elections. By layer that is 38.52 for schools, 4.17 for cities and 7.93 for counties.

Assessed value is 20% of market value, and millage is applied to that assessed figure. Schools receive about 80% of collections, counties about 15% and cities about 5%. Your own rate depends on the school district, city and county the house sits in, so two homes of equal value can get different bills. Read the assessor's notice for the actual millage on your parcel.

Counties reappraise every four years under Act 139 of 2023, and by 2028 every county will be on a four-year contract. Ask your assessor when your county's next reappraisal lands, since a reappraisal is when values jump.

Under Amendment 79, the taxable value of a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise only 5% a year after a reappraisal. Other real property is capped at 10% a year. Credits for homesteads and the age 65 or disabled freeze are covered in the homestead guide, so this page stays with assessment and collection.

A cap slows the climb of the taxable figure. It cannot stop a bill from growing when a school board raises millage.

sections.h2: Dates every Arkansas owner should know
sections.html:
The calendar below blends the statewide schedule with how Pulaski County runs its equalization process, which shows how one county applies the rules.

DateWhat happens
JulyAssessor mails notices of assessed value (Pulaski County)
August 1Equalization board holds its organizational meeting (Pulaski County)
Third Monday in AugustLast day to schedule a board hearing
September 30Regular board meetings end (Pulaski County)
Second Monday in OctoberLast day to petition county court
October 15Taxes due; unpaid bills turn delinquent
November 15County court must hear and rule on appeals
First business day of MarchCollection of the prior assessment year's bills begins

No assessment can be changed after the board's special session ends in November, so an owner who misses the August deadline should not expect a second chance that year.

The path runs from a conversation with the county assessor, to the county equalization board, to county court, and then to circuit court. The appeal statute, 26-27-318, controls the county court step.

  • The board hears only the current year's value and cannot take appeals of earlier years.
  • A county court petition goes to the county clerk, who assigns a case number. There is no filing fee.
  • You must have gone to the board first, unless you never received the required notice of a value change.
  • The county court has to publish notice at least a week before the hearing, or it lacks jurisdiction.
  • You carry the burden of proving true value by a preponderance of the evidence, and no presumption favors the assessor.
  • The court's written decision is due within 20 working days after the hearing and must tell you that you can go on to circuit court.

Many values change after informal talks alone, so the first conversation with the assessor is worth having. Before heading to circuit court, ask an attorney about the deadline.

Taxes unpaid after October 15 are delinquent and carry a 10% penalty plus daily interest on real estate. The collector publishes delinquent lists in a local newspaper.

The county does not hold a sale. Under Ark. Code 26-37-101, land still unpaid a year after the due date is certified to the Commissioner of State Lands by July 1 of the following year, and title vests in the state when certification arrives. The tax deed guide walks through what follows.

If you plan to sell, treat a delinquent bill as urgent rather than something to settle quietly later. After certification, the payoff goes through the state's office and the redemption deadline is firm.

sections.h2: The tax lien and who pays at a sale
sections.html:
The property tax lien arises on the first Monday of January of the year of assessment and lasts until the tax and penalties are paid. Section 26-34-101 ranks it ahead of judgments, executions, encumbrances and other liens, whenever those were created.

Between a grantor and a grantee, the statute holds the lien back until the last date set by law for the county clerk to deliver the tax books to the collector. That timing is why the tax bill is a closing item and not just the seller's private matter.

Collection runs from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A house sold in spring can close while the prior year's bill is unpaid. The title company can ask the collector for a status and pay what is owed from the seller's proceeds.

Before listing, confirm three things with the county: what you owe, what the next assessment will do, and whether any year is already delinquent.

  • Ask the collector for the current balance, with penalty and interest, by parcel number.
  • Read the latest assessor notice and see whether your county is reappraising this year.
  • If the August hearing date is behind you, calendar the second Monday in October for county court.
  • If a year is delinquent, find out whether it has been certified to the Commissioner of State Lands.

Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses, including houses with back taxes. Bring your latest tax statement and assessor notice, and the title company can pay the collector at closing.

faqs.q: When is Arkansas property tax due?
faqs.a: Taxes are collected from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. A payment after October 15 draws a 10% penalty, and delinquent real estate accrues interest daily.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to challenge my assessment?
faqs.a: Schedule an equalization board hearing by the third Monday in August. If you disagree with the board, file a county court petition by the second Monday in October. The board cannot hear earlier years.

faqs.q: Does it cost anything to appeal to county court?
faqs.a: No filing fee applies to the petition of appeal under 26-27-318. File with the county clerk, who assigns a case number, and the county court must rule by November 15.

faqs.q: How much can my homestead value rise in one year?
faqs.a: After a reappraisal, taxable value on a homestead owned by someone under 65 who is not disabled can rise 5% a year. Other real property is capped at 10% a year under Amendment 79.
School boards, city councils and county quorum courts set it during the assessment year, and the quorum court formally levies it. The statewide county average is 48.80 mills.
